title: The Basics
subtitle: The foundation everything else builds on
description: Before you can understand system design, you need to know how the pieces of a web application fit together. This module covers the five concepts that every app — from a simple to-do list to Instagram — relies on.

lessons.title: What is a server and what is a client?
lessons.description: The two halves of every app: the part you see (client) and the part you don't (server).

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
Every app has two parts:

- The **client** (or "front end") is what you see and interact with — the buttons, text, images, and forms in your browser or phone app.
- The **server** (or "back end") is a computer sitting somewhere in a data center that does the behind-the-scenes work — storing data, running logic, sending emails, processing payments.

When you use an app, your client talks to the server over the internet. The client asks for things ("show me my messages"), and the server responds ("here are your 12 unread messages").

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
If you're building with AI tools, you'll constantly hear "that's a front-end issue" or "the back end needs to handle that." Understanding this split helps you:

- Know **where a bug lives** — is the screen not showing data (front end) or is the data missing entirely (back end)?
- Give AI tools **better instructions** — "Build me a React component that calls the /messages endpoint" is much more useful than "build me a chat feature."
- Understand **security boundaries** — anything running on the client can be seen and modified by users. Sensitive logic (authentication, payments) must live on the server.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of a restaurant:

- **The dining room** is the client. It's where customers sit, read the menu, and place orders. It's designed to look nice and be easy to use.
- **The kitchen** is the server. It receives orders, has access to all the ingredients (data), does the actual cooking (logic), and sends the finished dish back.
- **The waiter** is the internet — carrying requests from the dining room to the kitchen and bringing back responses.

The customer never walks into the kitchen. They don't need to know how the food is made — they just need the right dish to show up. That's exactly how clients and servers work.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Every web or mobile app uses this model. Even "static" websites that look simple often have a server behind them for things like:

- Saving form submissions
- Loading user-specific content
- Processing payments
- Sending notifications

The only exceptions are purely static sites (like a digital business card) that have no dynamic behavior — no logins, no saved data, no personalization.

quiz.question: Where does the bug live?
quiz.scenario: A user reports: "When I click the 'Send Message' button, nothing happens. The button doesn't even look like it's loading." You check the server logs and there are no incoming requests from that user.

options.text: This is a front-end (client) issue
options.explanation: The server never received a request, which means the client never sent one. The button click handler is either broken or not wired up correctly. This is a client-side bug — the request never left the browser.

options.text: This is a back-end (server) issue
options.explanation: If the server has no record of the request, it never arrived. The problem is upstream — on the client side. If it were a server issue, you'd see the request arrive but fail to process.

options.text: This is a network issue
options.explanation: Possible but unlikely for a single user, and the clue is that the button doesn't even look like it's loading — suggesting the click handler itself isn't triggering the request. A network issue would typically show a loading state followed by an error.

lessons.title: What is an API and why does everything use them?
lessons.description: The contract between systems — how your front end talks to your back end (and how apps talk to each other).

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules for how two pieces of software talk to each other. It defines:

- What you can **ask for** ("get my messages," "create a new user," "delete this post")
- **How** to ask (what URL to call, what data to send)
- What you'll **get back** (the format of the response)

When your front end needs data from your back end, it doesn't reach into the database directly — it calls an API endpoint. When your app needs to send an email via SendGrid or charge a card via Stripe, it calls their APIs.

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
APIs are everywhere because they solve a fundamental problem: **different parts of a system need to communicate without knowing each other's internal details.**

As a builder, APIs matter because:

- Your front end talks to your back end through an API
- You'll integrate third-party services (Stripe, Twilio, OpenAI) through their APIs
- When AI tools generate code for you, understanding the API contract helps you verify it's correct
- When something breaks between systems, the API is usually where you look first

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of an API like a **restaurant menu**:

- The menu lists **what's available** (endpoints): appetizers, mains, desserts
- Each item has a **name and description** (documentation): "Caesar Salad — romaine, parmesan, croutons"
- You **order by name** (make a request): "I'll have the Caesar Salad"
- The kitchen **makes it and sends it back** (response): your salad arrives in a predictable format

You don't need to know how the kitchen makes the salad. You just need to know what's on the menu and how to order. That's an API.

In practice, an API call looks like this: your browser sends a request to `GET /api/messages?room=general` and your server responds with a list of messages in JSON format.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
You use APIs in almost every app:

- **Internal APIs**: Your front end calling your own back end
- **Third-party APIs**: Integrating external services (payment processing, email, AI models, maps)
- **Public APIs**: Letting other developers build on your platform (like Twitter's API or Stripe's API)

If two pieces of software need to exchange data, there's an API in between.

quiz.question: Which is the API call?
quiz.scenario: You're building a weather app. You need to show the current temperature for a user's city. Your app doesn't have weather data — it needs to get it from a weather service.

options.text: Your app calls GET api.weather.com/current?city=seattle and displays the result
options.explanation: This is an API call to a third-party service. Your app asks the weather API for data (the request), gets back a structured response (temperature, conditions, etc.), and displays it. Your app doesn't need to know how they measure weather — it just uses the API.

options.text: Your app looks up the temperature in its own database
options.explanation: Your app doesn't have weather data — that's the whole point. You need an external API to get it. This is a common pattern: your app combines data from your own database with data from external APIs.

options.text: Your app scrapes the weather website and extracts the number
options.explanation: Web scraping (reading a website's HTML to extract data) technically works but is fragile, unreliable, and often against a site's terms of service. APIs exist specifically so you don't have to do this — they give you structured data in a predictable format.

lessons.title: What is a database and why can't I just use a spreadsheet?
lessons.description: Where your app's data lives permanently — and why it's not just a fancy spreadsheet.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
A **database** is a system for storing, organizing, and retrieving data. It's where your app keeps everything that needs to persist: user accounts, messages, orders, settings, content.

Unlike a spreadsheet, a database is designed to:
- Handle **thousands of simultaneous readers and writers** without corrupting data
- Find specific data **instantly** even among millions of records
- Ensure data is **never lost**, even if the power goes out mid-write
- Enforce **rules about your data** (e.g., "every user must have a unique email")

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
If your app stores any user data at all, it needs a database. Understanding databases helps you:

- **Design your data model** — what tables/collections do you need? What fields? AI tools can generate this, but you need to verify it makes sense.
- **Diagnose slow pages** — often the fix is a database issue (missing index, loading too much data, N+1 queries)
- **Choose the right database** — not all databases work the same way, and the wrong choice can be painful to fix later
- **Talk to engineers credibly** — "the query is slow because there's no index on the user_id column" earns a lot of respect

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of a database like a **library**:

- **Tables** are like different sections (Fiction, Science, History) — each one holds a specific type of data
- **Rows** are like individual books — each one is a record (a user, an order, a message)
- **Columns** are like the properties of each book (title, author, ISBN, publish date)
- **Indexes** are like the card catalog — they let you find a specific book without searching every shelf
- **Queries** are like asking the librarian: "Find me all science books published after 2020, sorted by author name"

A spreadsheet is like a library with one room, no catalog, and one librarian. It works great for 100 books. But add 100,000 books and 50 people all asking for different ones simultaneously? You need a real library system. That's a database.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Use a database when your app needs to:

- **Remember things between sessions** (user accounts, saved preferences)
- **Share data between users** (messages, posts, comments)
- **Handle multiple users at once** (any multi-user app)
- **Query data flexibly** ("show me all orders over $50 from last month")

You might NOT need a database for: a static landing page, a calculator tool, or a single-user app that only needs browser storage.

quiz.question: Spreadsheet or database?
quiz.scenario: You're building a marketplace app where sellers list products and buyers purchase them. At launch you expect 500 sellers and 5,000 products, growing to 10,000 sellers in a year. Multiple people will be browsing, searching, and buying simultaneously.

options.text: Database — concurrent access, search, and data relationships require it
options.explanation: A marketplace has concurrent users reading and writing data simultaneously (buyers browsing while sellers update listings), complex queries (search, filter, sort), and relationships between data (users ↔ orders ↔ products). This is exactly what databases are built for.

options.text: Spreadsheet — 5,000 products isn't that much data
options.explanation: It's not about the amount of data — it's about concurrency and complexity. Even 100 products would need a database if 50 people are simultaneously browsing, searching, filtering, and purchasing. A spreadsheet can't handle multiple writers safely, and searching is slow.

lessons.title: HTTP requests: What happens when you type a URL?
lessons.description: The invisible conversation your browser has every time you visit a website.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules your browser uses to communicate with servers. Every time you visit a website, click a link, or submit a form, your browser sends an **HTTP request** and the server sends back an **HTTP response**.

The main types of HTTP requests (called "methods") are:

- **GET** — "Give me something" (loading a page, fetching data)
- **POST** — "Here's something new" (submitting a form, creating a record)
- **PUT/PATCH** — "Update this" (editing a profile, changing settings)
- **DELETE** — "Remove this" (deleting a post, removing a friend)

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
HTTP is the language of the web. Understanding it helps you:

- **Debug API issues** — "I'm getting a 404" means the URL is wrong. "I'm getting a 500" means the server crashed. These numbers are HTTP status codes and they tell you *exactly* what went wrong.
- **Understand what AI builds** — when AI generates code that calls `fetch('/api/users', { method: 'POST' })`, you know it's creating a new user, not reading one.
- **Read documentation** — every API's docs describe endpoints using HTTP methods: `GET /users`, `POST /orders`, `DELETE /posts/:id`.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
When you type `google.com` into your browser, here's the invisible conversation:

1. **Your browser** sends a request: "Hey google.com, GET me your homepage"
2. The request travels across the internet to **Google's server**
3. Google's server processes the request and sends back a **response**: the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript that make up the page
4. **Your browser** receives the response and renders it on screen

This whole round trip takes milliseconds. And it happens hundreds of times as the page loads — for images, fonts, scripts, and data.

The key status codes to know:
- **200** — OK, here's what you asked for
- **301/302** — This moved, go look over there (redirect)
- **400** — You sent a bad request (missing data, wrong format)
- **401** — You're not logged in
- **403** — You're logged in but don't have permission
- **404** — This doesn't exist
- **500** — The server broke (not your fault)

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Every web interaction uses HTTP:

- Loading any webpage → GET requests
- Submitting a signup form → POST request
- Updating your profile → PUT/PATCH request
- Clicking "Delete my account" → DELETE request
- Your app calling Stripe's API to charge a card → POST request to Stripe's server

Understanding HTTP methods and status codes is like understanding road signs — you need them to navigate.

quiz.question: What's the status code telling you?
quiz.scenario: You're testing your app and try to load a user's profile page. The browser shows a blank page. You open the developer console and see: `GET /api/users/42 → 401 Unauthorized`.

options.text: The user isn't logged in or the authentication token is missing/expired
options.explanation: A 401 means the server doesn't know who you are. The request reached the server fine, but you didn't prove your identity. Either the user isn't logged in, or the auth token in the request is missing, expired, or invalid.

options.text: User #42 doesn't exist in the database
options.explanation: That would be a 404 (Not Found). A 401 is specifically about authentication — the server is saying "I don't know who's asking," not "I can't find what you're asking for."

options.text: The server crashed while processing the request
options.explanation: A server crash would return a 500 (Internal Server Error). A 401 is a deliberate response — the server is working correctly and intentionally rejecting the request because authentication is missing.

lessons.title: JSON: The language computers use to talk to each other
lessons.description: The simple data format that powers almost every API on the internet.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for representing structured data. It's how your front end and back end exchange information, and it's what almost every API in the world uses.

JSON looks like this:

```json
{
  "name": "Lucy",
  "role": "Product Manager",
  "skills": ["strategy", "design", "vibe-coding"],
  "isAwesome": true
}
```

That's it. Curly braces for objects, square brackets for lists, quotes around text, and simple values like numbers and true/false. If you can read a form, you can read JSON.

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
JSON is the lingua franca of the web. When you:

- Call an API → you get JSON back
- Send data to a server → you send JSON
- Read configuration files → often JSON
- Look at AI model responses → JSON

Being comfortable reading JSON means you can inspect API responses, debug data issues, and understand what your app is actually sending and receiving. When AI generates an API for you, the data flowing through it is almost certainly JSON.

sections.heading: how
when
sections.content:
You encounter JSON constantly:

- **API responses**: `fetch('/api/user')` returns JSON
- **Configuration**: `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` — your project's settings
- **AI model APIs**: When you call Claude's API, you send and receive JSON
- **Database exports**: Data dumps are often in JSON format

You don't need to write JSON from scratch often (AI tools handle that), but you need to **read** it to verify things are working and debug when they're not.

quiz.question: Read the JSON
quiz.scenario:
Your app calls an API and gets this response:

```json
{ "status": "error", "code": 422, "message": "Email already exists", "field": "email" }
```

A user reports they can't sign up. What's the issue?

options.text: Someone already registered with that email address
options.explanation: The JSON tells you exactly what happened: status is "error", the message says "Email already exists", and the problematic field is "email". The 422 status code means "the data you sent is valid format but can't be processed" — in this case, because the email is taken. You could show the user a helpful message or suggest they try logging in instead.

options.text: The server is down
options.explanation: If the server were down, you wouldn't get a structured JSON response at all — you'd get a connection error or a 500 status code. This is a 422, which means the server is working fine but rejecting the data for a specific reason.

options.text: The email format is invalid
options.explanation: Close, but read the message carefully — it says "Email already exists," not "Email is invalid." The format is fine; the email just belongs to an existing account. JSON gives you precise error information if you read it.

lessons.title: Non-Functional Requirements: The invisible qualities that matter most
lessons.description: The "-ilities" that make or break your system.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
Functional requirements are WHAT your app does (users can sign up, place orders). Non-functional requirements (NFRs) are HOW WELL it does them. The main ones:

- **Availability** — what percentage of the time is the system up? 99.9% = ~8 hours downtime/year
- **Reliability** — does the system produce correct results consistently?
- **Scalability** — can it handle growth in users, data, traffic?
- **Maintainability** — how easy is it to change, debug, and extend?
- **Fault Tolerance** — does it keep working when components fail?

These are often called the "-ilities."

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Engineers and PMs often focus on features and forget NFRs until something breaks. Understanding NFRs helps you:

- Set realistic SLAs with customers
- Prioritize engineering investments (should we build a new feature or improve uptime?)
- Ask the right questions in design reviews ("what happens if this service goes down?")
- Understand why engineers push back on "simple" feature requests (the feature is simple, but making it reliable at scale isn't)

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Analogy: building a house. Functional requirements are the rooms, kitchen, bathrooms — what the house HAS. Non-functional requirements are the structural integrity, insulation, plumbing reliability, fire resistance — how WELL the house performs.

A house can have a beautiful kitchen (feature) but terrible insulation (NFR), making it miserable to live in.

NFRs often conflict with each other:

- Optimizing for **availability** (more redundancy) increases cost
- Optimizing for **consistency** (strong guarantees) reduces performance

A PM's job is to help the team decide which NFRs matter most for THEIR users and make conscious tradeoffs.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
You should think about NFRs when scoping any feature:

- What uptime do users expect?
- How fast should it be?
- What happens during a traffic spike?
- What happens if a component fails?

Different products have different NFR priorities:

- A **banking app** prioritizes reliability and consistency
- A **social media feed** prioritizes availability and performance
- An **internal admin tool** can tolerate lower availability

quiz.question: Which non-functional requirement should you prioritize?
quiz.scenario: You're a PM at a fintech startup launching a money transfer feature. The engineering lead asks you to rank priorities: fast transfers (low latency), always-available service (high availability), or guaranteed correct balances (strong consistency). During your beta, a bug caused one user to see an incorrect balance for 3 seconds, which triggered a support escalation and a compliance review.

options.text: Strong consistency — correct balances are non-negotiable for financial products
options.explanation: For financial transactions, showing incorrect balances even briefly can violate regulations and destroy trust. Users will tolerate a transfer taking 2 seconds instead of 200ms, and brief planned maintenance windows, but they will NOT tolerate seeing wrong numbers in their account.

options.text: High availability — the service should never go down
options.explanation: Availability matters, but for a financial product, showing incorrect data is worse than brief downtime. Users understand scheduled maintenance. They don't understand seeing the wrong balance. The beta incident — a compliance review over 3 seconds of wrong data — shows where the real risk is.

options.text: Low latency — fast transfers create the best user experience
options.explanation: Speed is nice, but users expect financial transfers to take a moment. Nobody panics if a transfer takes 2 seconds. But everyone panics if their balance looks wrong. The compliance review triggered by the beta bug tells you exactly which NFR carries the highest stakes.

lessons.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation: How to size a problem in 5 minutes
lessons.description: Roughly sizing problems before building solutions.

sections.heading: what
sections.content: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is the practice of making rough calculations to understand the scale of a problem before designing a solution. You don't need exact numbers — you need the right **order of magnitude**. Is this a problem that involves thousands of requests or millions? Gigabytes of storage or terabytes? Knowing the ballpark changes the architecture completely.

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Estimation helps you:

- **Catch unrealistic proposals early** — "we need to handle 1 million concurrent users" — do you though?
- **Choose the right tools** — a problem at 100 requests/second needs a very different solution than 100,000
- **Have credible conversations** with engineers about capacity planning
- **Understand cost implications** before committing to an architecture

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Analogy: estimating how much food to order for a party. You don't need to know exactly how many slices of pizza each person eats. You need to know: how many people (50? 500?), roughly how much each person eats (2-3 slices), and from that you can estimate pizzas needed.

**Key numbers to know for tech estimation:**

- 1 million seconds ~ 11.5 days
- 1 billion seconds ~ 31.7 years
- A typical web page is 2-5 MB
- A [[glossary:database|database]] row is roughly 100 bytes to 1 KB
- A typical [[glossary:server|server]] handles 1,000-10,000 requests per second
- 1 TB of cloud storage costs about $20-25/month

**The basic formula:** Start with users, estimate actions per user per day, multiply out to get requests per second (total daily actions / 86,400 seconds).

**Example:** 100,000 users x 10 actions/day = 1 million actions/day = about 12 requests per second average, maybe 50-100 at peak. One server handles that easily.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Use estimation:

- **Before any architecture discussion** — how big is this problem actually?
- **Before choosing infrastructure** — do we need a distributed system or will one server do?
- **When evaluating vendor proposals** — is this service overkill or right-sized?
- **When scoping MVP vs. full-scale solutions** — can we start simple and scale later?

You don't need to be precise — being within 10x of the real answer is usually enough to make the right architectural choice.

quiz.question: Does this scale justify the solution?
quiz.scenario: Your team is planning a photo-sharing app. The PM estimates 50,000 daily active users, each uploading an average of 2 photos per day. Each photo is about 3 MB. An engineer proposes building a custom distributed file storage system from scratch to handle the load. You do the math: 50,000 x 2 x 3 MB = 300 GB per day, about 9 TB per month.

options.text: Use a managed blob storage service like S3 — 9 TB/month is routine for cloud storage
options.explanation: 9 TB/month is well within what any cloud storage service handles trivially for under $200/month. Building custom distributed storage for this scale is massive over-engineering. The estimation revealed the problem is much smaller than it sounded.

options.text: Build the custom system — photo storage will be a core competitive advantage
options.explanation: Storage is a commodity, not a differentiator. At 9 TB/month, managed services like S3 handle this effortlessly and cheaply. Building custom distributed storage would take months of engineering time for a problem that's already solved. Your competitive advantage is in the product, not the file system.

options.text: Delay the decision — we need exact numbers before choosing an approach
options.explanation: That's the whole point of back-of-the-envelope estimation: you don't need exact numbers. Whether the real number is 5 TB or 15 TB per month, the answer is the same — use managed storage. Waiting for precision wastes time when the order of magnitude already tells you the answer.
